name: Reed v. Hoy
court: Ninth Circuit (from the District of Oregon)
topic: Fourth Amendment deadly force, Graham objective reasonableness applied retroactively, jury instruction requiring malice rejected, shooting in self-defense is a seizure, Oregon duty to retreat instruction refused
summary: A deputy investigating a domestic disturbance shot a homeowner who advanced on him with a splitting maul after refusing repeated orders to put it down. The jury found for the deputy under an instruction that required the shooting to be intentional, unjustified, unprovoked, and brutal, and asked whether the deputy acted in good faith or maliciously. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that under Graham v. Connor the shooting was a Fourth Amendment seizure to be judged by objective reasonableness, with no place for the officer's intent. It also held the trial court properly refused an instruction that Oregon law required the deputy to retreat. It is taught as an objective test case.
coverage: The opinion was read in full from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F2/891/891.F2d.1421.87-4324.html. That file is headed 891 F.2d 1421, carries docket No. 87-4324, and states on its face: "Decided Dec. 15, 1989. As Amended on Denial of Rehearing and Rehearing En Banc July 18, 1990." The text read is therefore the amended opinion.

The 909 F.2d 324 report of the amended opinion, which is the citation used in course materials, is not present in the archive's volume 909 directory (the listing jumps from 909 F.2d 320 to 909 F.2d 332). CourtListener and Justia were not reachable through this session's network. The 909 F.2d 324 citation is corroborated by the Ninth Circuit's own en banc opinion in Smith v. City of Hemet, 394 F.3d 689 (9th Cir. 2005), which quotes and cites "Reed v. Hoy, 909 F.2d 324, 329 (9th Cir.1989), cert. denied, 501 U.S. 1250" and which was read for this library from the same archive. The quoted sentence appears verbatim in the text read for this brief. Page numbers within 909 F.2d were not verified, so no pin cites are given.
Smith v. City of Hemet also reports that certiorari was denied at 501 U.S. 1250 (1991). That was not independently verified.
The trial record, the Rinker instruction as given, and Reed's requested instruction are known only as the Ninth Circuit quoted them.

Course note for Dr. Sowards: the October 2026 revision describes Reed v. Hoy as an objective test case and says it is not a no duty to retreat case. The principal holding is indeed the Graham objective test. The opinion does, however, contain a separate Part III.B holding that, under Oregon law, the duty to retreat does not extend to police officers performing their official function, and that the trial court did not err in refusing Reed's duty to retreat instruction. The court noted in a footnote that Reed did not argue that the Fourth Amendment itself requires an officer to retreat. The retreat ruling is a matter of Oregon state law and does not establish a federal constitutional rule; for California officers the no retreat rule comes from Penal Code section 835a.
California Penal Code section 835a was not read for this brief. Statements about its no retreat rule and its definition of retreat come from Dr. Sowards' course materials, which quote the statute.

Citation as written in the brief: 909 F.2d 324 (9th Cir. 1989, amended 1990). The source read gave it as: 891 F.2d 1421 (9th Cir. 1989), as amended on denial of rehearing and rehearing en banc July 18, 1990 (the amended opinion is reported at 909 F.2d 324).
facts:
On August 18, 1984, Deputy Daniel Hoy of the Douglas County, Oregon, Sheriff's Office was dispatched to Robert Reed's residence to investigate a reported domestic disturbance. When Hoy arrived, Reed was crouched outside the house with his back to the deputy. Hoy greeted him and said he was investigating a possible crime, and asked to speak with Mrs. Reed. Reed angrily replied that his wife did not want to speak to Hoy and told him to get off his property. Hoy said he was investigating a possible family disturbance and would leave as soon as he spoke with Mrs. Reed.

After a further brief verbal exchange, Reed picked up a 36 inch bamboo stick used to stake flowers and again demanded that Hoy leave. Hoy drew his nightstick and again asked to see Mrs. Reed. Reed walked to the porch, put down the bamboo stick, and picked up a splitting maul. He advanced on Hoy, again demanding that he leave. Reed testified that he was very angry and that his purpose was to scare Hoy. Hoy retreated, walking backwards, and told Reed to put down the maul. Reed refused.

Hoy kept walking backwards and Reed kept advancing, closing the distance. Hoy again asked Reed to put the maul down. When Reed refused and continued to advance, Hoy drew his service revolver, pointed it at Reed, and again told him to put the maul down. Hoy testified that Reed continued to advance, grabbed the maul with both hands, and raised it in a threatening manner. Hoy shot Reed in the chest.

Reed sued under section 1983, alleging Hoy used excessive force in violation of his constitutional rights, and alleging the county failed to train Hoy adequately in the use of force. The case was tried to a jury. The court instructed the jury, based on the Ninth Circuit's earlier decision in Rinker v. County of Napa, that to prevail on his due process claim Reed had to prove the shooting "was intentional, unjustified, unprovoked, and brutal," and that the jury was to decide whether Hoy shot Reed "in a good faith effort to protect himself or did so maliciously and for the very purpose of injuring" him. The court refused Reed's alternative instruction, which would have told the jury that an officer may use the force a reasonable person would think necessary to accomplish lawful objectives and no more. The court also refused Reed's request for an instruction that under Oregon law Hoy had a duty to retreat before using deadly force. The jury found for the defendants. Reed appealed, challenging the instructions and evidentiary rulings.
holding:
Reversed and remanded for a new trial.

The standard. The Rinker instruction asked the jury whether Hoy acted in good faith or maliciously. The court held that instruction "inconsistent with the standards recently enunciated by the Supreme Court" in Graham v. Connor, which was decided after the trial. Under Graham, all claims that officers used excessive force, deadly or not, in the course of an arrest, investigatory stop, or other seizure of a free citizen are analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard rather than substantive due process, and subjective concepts like malice and sadism have no place in that inquiry. The court applied Graham retroactively, reasoning that the Supreme Court described its rule as making explicit what was implicit in Garner, that retroactive application furthers the Fourth Amendment's purposes, and that neither Hoy nor the county could have relied on the Rinker standard in deciding how to act.

A self-defense shooting is a seizure. Hoy argued Garner applies only when deadly force is used to make an arrest. The court rejected that. Applying Brower v. County of Inyo, it held a seizure is a governmental termination of freedom of movement through means intentionally applied, and that Hoy's shooting met every element: Hoy was a government actor, the shot ended Reed's movement, and Hoy intended to shoot Reed to stop his advance. "Whether the application of deadly force is for the purpose of effectuating an arrest or other stop, or for the purpose of self-defense, it is an acquisition of physical control by a law enforcement official that implicates the victim's fourth amendment interest to be free from unreasonable seizures."

Plain error and the new trial. Because excessive force claims arising before or during arrest are analyzed exclusively under the Fourth Amendment, and because the Rinker standard and the Graham standard "differ dramatically," giving the Rinker instruction was plain error. The court rejected Hoy's argument that his actions were reasonable as a matter of law: "While a jury may find that Hoy acted reasonably, Reed presented sufficient evidence that a reasonable jury could rule in his favor." On retrial the jury must decide whether the seizure was reasonable by balancing the nature and quality of the intrusion against the governmental interests, considering the severity of the crime, whether the suspect posed an immediate threat to the safety of the officer or others, and whether he was actively resisting or attempting to evade by flight.

The duty to retreat instruction. Because a new trial was likely, the court also addressed Reed's argument that the trial court should have instructed the jury that, under Oregon law, Hoy had a duty to retreat before using deadly force. The court held this contention "has no merit." The Oregon statute and the Oregon Supreme Court decision Reed relied on involved ordinary citizens. Reed "has not cited to this court a single case from any jurisdiction suggesting that police officers have the same duty to retreat as ordinary citizens," and such a duty "may be inconsistent with police officers' duty to the public to pursue investigations of criminal activity." Noting that a proposed Oregon code provision discussed by the Oregon Supreme Court had expressly excluded peace officers from any duty to retreat, the court concluded that "under Oregon law, the duty to retreat does not extend to police officers performing their official function." The trial court did not err in refusing the instruction. In a footnote the court observed that state law is often relevant to Fourth Amendment reasonableness, so if Oregon had required retreat that would have been an important factor, but Reed did not argue that the Fourth Amendment, apart from Oregon law, requires an officer to retreat before using deadly force.
notDecided:
Whether Hoy's shooting was reasonable. The court said a jury could find either way and ordered a new trial under the correct standard. No court in this opinion found the shooting excessive or justified.

Whether the Fourth Amendment itself ever requires an officer to retreat before using deadly force. Reed did not make that argument, and the court said so in a footnote. The retreat holding is a ruling about Oregon law.

The failure to train claim against Douglas County. The opinion recites the claim but does not analyze it.

Whether Hoy's conduct before the shooting was itself a seizure. The court said it did not need to decide that because the shooting was a seizure.

The evidentiary rulings Reed challenged. The opinion addresses only the jury instructions.
inPractice:
The lesson of Reed v. Hoy is the standard, not the retreat. A jury had already found for the deputy, but the verdict was thrown out because the jury was asked the wrong question. Good faith, malice, and intent to injure are not the test. The test is whether a reasonable officer in Hoy's position, facing a man advancing with a splitting maul who ignored repeated commands, would have used that force. An officer's state of mind cannot save an objectively unreasonable use of force, and bad motives cannot condemn an objectively reasonable one.

The case also settles a point that matters for every self-defense shooting: the Fourth Amendment applies. An officer who shoots to stop an attack, not to make an arrest, has still seized the person and will be judged under Graham.

On retreat, the court held only that Oregon law did not impose on an on duty officer the duty to retreat that Oregon imposed on private citizens, so the deputy was entitled to have that instruction kept from the jury. The court said nothing about whether the Fourth Amendment requires retreat, because the plaintiff never argued it. Note also what the deputy actually did: he retreated, walking backwards, and repeated his commands several times before firing. His movement and his commands are part of why a jury could find for him under either standard.

Dr. Sowards' course materials historically listed Reed v. Hoy as a no duty to retreat case. The October 2026 revision reclassified it as an objective test case, and that is how the course now teaches it: officers are judged on what a reasonable officer would do, not on their intent. For California officers the rule that an officer need not retreat or desist because of resistance, and that retreat does not mean tactical repositioning, comes from Penal Code section 835a, not from Reed v. Hoy.
trainIt:
Use Reed to teach the standard the jury will apply. Give students the two instructions side by side: the Rinker instruction (intentional, unjustified, unprovoked, brutal; good faith versus malice) and the Graham instruction (nature and quality of the intrusion balanced against the governmental interest; severity of the crime, immediate threat, active resistance or flight). Have them explain why the same facts can produce a different verdict under each, and why the Ninth Circuit called the difference dramatic. The point for the officer is that honest intentions are not a defense and that the report must give the jury the objective facts.

Run the encounter as a decision drill. A domestic disturbance call, a hostile homeowner who tells you to leave, a bamboo stake, then a splitting maul, then an advance that closes distance while you move backward and repeat commands. At each step, students state what a reasonable officer would perceive and what options remain: distance, cover, verbal commands, intermediate tools, deadly force. Emphasize that Hoy's repeated commands and his backward movement are facts a jury weighs on the immediate threat factor.

Teach retreat accurately. Reed v. Hoy held only that Oregon law imposed no duty to retreat on an on duty officer. California officers get the no retreat rule from Penal Code section 835a, which also says retreat does not mean tactical repositioning or other de-escalation. Train students to reposition for distance and cover when it is safe, because that is what Hoy did and because it strengthens both the tactical outcome and the reasonableness case, while making clear that the law does not require them to abandon a lawful task in the face of resistance.

Teach the posture: a defense verdict reversed on instructional error and sent back for a new trial. No court decided whether the shot was reasonable.
caution: The text read is the amended opinion as republished in the archive's 891 F.2d 1421 file; the 909 F.2d 324 report itself was not available, so pin cites to 909 F.2d are not given. The facts are the trial record as the Ninth Circuit summarized it, and the reasonableness of the shooting was never decided in this opinion. The duty to retreat holding is a ruling on Oregon law only.

applications.title: Intent is not the test
applications.body: The jury was told to decide whether the deputy acted in good faith or maliciously. That was reversible error. Under Graham, force is judged by what a reasonable officer would do under the circumstances. Write reports that give the objective facts, not your motives.

applications.title: Self-defense shootings are seizures
applications.body: Hoy argued Garner applied only to force used to make an arrest. The court held that shooting a man to stop his advance is an intentional acquisition of physical control and therefore a Fourth Amendment seizure, whatever the officer's purpose.

applications.title: What the court said about retreat, and what it did not
applications.body: The court held that under Oregon law an on duty officer has no duty to retreat before using deadly force, so the plaintiff's requested instruction was properly refused. It did not decide whether the Fourth Amendment ever requires retreat, because that argument was never made. California's no retreat rule is in Penal Code section 835a.

applications.title: Commands and distance count
applications.body: Hoy walked backwards and told Reed to put the maul down several times, escalating from a nightstick to a drawn firearm, before he fired. Those facts go to the immediate threat factor and to whether the force was reasonable.

applications.title: A verdict is not the end
applications.body: The deputy won at trial and lost on appeal because of the instruction. The case went back for a new trial under Graham. Nothing in the opinion decides whether the shooting was excessive.

quiz.q: Why did the Ninth Circuit reverse the defense verdict in Reed v. Hoy?
options: Because the deputy had a duty to retreat and did not
Because the jury was instructed to decide whether the deputy acted in good faith or maliciously, which is not the Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness test required by Graham v. Connor
Because the shooting was excessive as a matter of law
Because the county failed to train the deputy
quiz.teach: Graham makes the test objective reasonableness; malice and sadism have no place in it. The court applied Graham retroactively and held that giving the Rinker instruction was plain error.

quiz.q: What did the court hold about the plaintiff's requested duty to retreat instruction?
options: The instruction should have been given because all persons must retreat before using deadly force
The Fourth Amendment requires officers to retreat when they safely can
Under Oregon law the duty to retreat does not extend to police officers performing their official function, so the trial court properly refused it
The court did not address the instruction
quiz.teach: This was a ruling on Oregon law. The court noted that Reed did not argue that the Fourth Amendment itself requires retreat, so the opinion does not establish any federal constitutional rule on retreat.

quiz.q: Did the Ninth Circuit decide whether Deputy Hoy's shooting was reasonable?
options: Yes, it held the shooting reasonable as a matter of law
Yes, it held the shooting excessive
No, it said a jury could find either way and ordered a new trial under the Graham standard
quiz.teach: The court rejected Hoy's argument that he was entitled to a directed verdict, saying a jury might find he acted reasonably but Reed had presented enough evidence for a jury to rule for him. The merits were left for retrial.
